title: The main disciplines
summary: A short guide to Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting, plus Trap and Skeet: what they share and how they differ.

body.html: Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ imitates hunting. Shooting stands, the marked spots you shoot from, are set out over natural ground: in fields, by woods, on slopes. Targets fly the way a partridge, a duck or a pheasant would, or roll like a hare. Each layout, a group of stands, gives 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles (a double is two targets, so 10 more). The two targets of a double fly together or one after the other.

Compak® Sporting is the compact version. Everything happens on one field with 6 traps lettered A to F and 5 shooting stations in a line. The shooter moves through all five stations and shoots 5 targets at each, 25 per round. A Compak field needs little space, so it is easy for a club to build one.

html.sporting: You walk a course from stand to stand, and each stand has its own targets. A double can be on report, where your first shot releases the second target, or simultaneous, where both fly at once. A rafale is two targets from the same trap, one right after the other.
html.compak: You stay on one field and, after each turn, move one station to the right. A double is on report, where your first shot releases the second target, or simultaneous, where both fly at once.

body.html: International competitions in both disciplines are usually 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25. In both, you may fire two shots at a single target: if the first shot misses, the second can still break it.

Trap is a different family of disciplines. The shooter stands at one of five stations in a row, and targets fly away out of a trench (a sunken pit in front of the stations) at changing angles. The shooter does not know exactly where the next target will go. In Olympic Trap, two shots may be fired at each target.

In Skeet the targets come from two houses (small buildings that hold the traps) facing each other, a high one and a low one. The shooter moves between stations on a half-circle between the houses, plus one in the middle. The trajectories do not change, so precise, well-drilled technique matters a lot.

Olympic Trap and Skeet are on the Olympic programme and belong to another international federation, ISSF. But FITASC also has trap and skeet disciplines of its own, such as Universal Trench and Universal Skeet. The ClayArena Academy is mostly about Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting. The basics are shared by all disciplines: safety, the gun mount (bringing the gun to cheek and shoulder) and reading the target.

key_points.html: Sporting™: a course over natural ground; each layout gives 25 targets.
Compak® Sporting: one field with 6 traps lettered A to F and 5 shooting stations in a line.
An international competition is usually 200 targets, shot in rounds of 25; you may fire twice at a single target.
In Trap targets fly away from the shooter; in Skeet they cross between two houses.

did_you_know.html: Compak® Sporting was created in 1989 and adopted by FITASC in 1991.

quiz.q: How many targets does one Sporting™ layout give?
quiz.explain: Each layout gives 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles (a double is two targets, so 10 more).

quiz.q: How many traps are there on one Compak field?

options.text: Two, a high and a low one

quiz.explain: A Compak® Sporting field has 6 traps lettered A to F and 5 shooting stations in a line.

quiz.q: In which discipline do targets come from two houses, a high one and a low one?
quiz.explain: Skeet has a high house and a low house, with the stations on a half-circle between them.
